**Other pollution externalities and education.** A parallel economics literature documents comparable long-run human capital costs from other pollutants, most prominently particulate matter and extreme heat. @rothAirPollutionEducational2017 and @hospidoAirPollutionReview2023 frame these costs as additive to, not subsumed by, conventional health-cost accounting of pollution, and @nguyentuand.EffectAirPollution2026 quantifies the accumulated causal evidence in the first meta-analysis of the field, pooling 28 studies and 62 effect sizes to an average achievement penalty of -0.022 SD, roughly a third larger for boys than girls. Within this body of work, a cluster of studies traces long-run schooling and earnings losses to early-life exposure. @sandersWhatDoesntKill2012 exploits the pollution decline caused by the 1980s Texas industrial recession and finds that prenatal exposure to total suspended particulates lowers later high-stakes test scores, while @bharadwajGrayMattersFetal2017 use sibling comparisons in Santiago to show that fetal exposure to carbon monoxide reduces fourth-grade math and language scores, and @chenIndustrializationPollutionLongterm2025 exploits upwind/downwind exposure during China's 1950s industrialization to show that moving from the 25th to 75th percentile of early-life exposure costs roughly 0.11 years of schooling, a magnitude the author argues rivals several canonical determinants of attainment. @isenEveryBreathYou2017 exploit the staggered county rollout of the 1970 Clean Air Act and find that reduced particulate exposure in the year of birth raises earnings and labor-force participation at age 30, and @colmerGrandkidsArentAlright2020 extend this logic across generations, showing that children of parents exposed to higher particulate pollution attain less education themselves, with similar effects for adopted and biological children, consistent with a channel operating through reduced parental resources rather than biology alone.

A second, larger set of studies isolates shorter-run, quasi-random pollution and temperature shocks to identify contemporaneous effects on schooling outcomes, and has increasingly diversified the settings in which the relationship is tested. In the United States, @marcotteSomethingAirAir2017 and @heisselDoesPollutionDrive2022 find that particulate matter and traffic-related pollution lower test scores and raise absences and behavioral incidents among schoolchildren, while @currieDoesPollutionIncrease2009 and @liuSevereAirPollution2018 show pollution raises school absenteeism directly, a channel distinct from any effect on cognitive performance conditional on attending. Exploiting variation specifically on the day of high-stakes assessments, @ebensteinLongRunEconomicConsequences2016 show that transitory PM2.5 exposure during Israeli matriculation exams lowers scores and, propagating through college admissions, adult wages a decade later, a design subsequently replicated for university exams in London [@rothEffectIndoorAir2018] and São Paulo [@bediParticlePollutionCognition2021] and for China's national college entrance exam [@graffzivinUnintendedImpactsAgricultural2020]. Newer natural experiments push this design into settings less confounded by traffic or industry and into new outcome margins: @hallidayVogUsingVolcanic2025 uses Kilauea's volcanic "vog" to show the test-score penalty is at least three times larger for the poorest students, and @valdesCanLowEmission2025 finds Madrid's low-emission zone raised university-entrance scores by 0.17 SD inside the zone, with spillovers just outside it and larger gains for students exposed earlier and longer. Two recent studies complicate the emerging consensus with informative nulls: @andersenAirPollutionCognition2024, using Danish register and 1km-grid pollution data, find PM2.5 harms math more than reading even at very low pollution levels but detect no heterogeneity by health, socioeconomic status, or cumulative exposure — suggesting the acute effect is closer to universal than concentrated among the vulnerable — while @merkusHoldYourBreath2024, studying Colombian exit exams, finds a same-day score penalty that does not persist into long-run college completion, a caveat against assuming every short-run effect compounds. Complementary work on extreme heat finds a similar pattern: @parkLearningInhibitedHeat2020 show that hot school days and hot exam days both reduce standardized test performance and, cumulatively, long-run educational attainment, and @borzinoHeatAirPollution2026 finds in 59 countries' PISA data that heat and PM2.5 compound one another, translating the joint loss into an illustrative 1.6–3.2% lifetime-earnings penalty that is more than twice as large in low- and middle-income countries — evidence that pollution and heat operate as related, and possibly compounding, threats to human capital formation through the same underlying disruption of same-day cognitive performance.

A final set of studies turns from identifying harm to identifying mechanisms and remedies. On mitigation, @gilraineAirFiltersPollution2025 and @ferroCloudedMindsAir2026 show that indoor air filtration and school ventilation/air-conditioning systems substantially attenuate pollution's cognitive cost, and two recent randomized trials push this evidence toward experimental confirmation: @bonanEffectAirPurifiers2024 find classroom air purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by 32% and reduce absenteeism by 12.5%, with the benefit largest precisely when outdoor pollution is low, while @blakesleeCleanAirClassroom2026 provide some of the first experimental evidence that purifiers improve directly measured child cognition rather than only attendance, and @maMitigatingCognitiveDeficits2025 show a prenatal nutrition intervention can partly offset pollution-linked cognitive deficits. On mechanisms, two studies identify overlooked channels through which pollution depresses local human capital: @martinDownwindBusLane2026 shows schools downwind of bus rapid transit corridors score measurably lower, implicating transit infrastructure itself as an unpriced human-capital externality, and @chenAirPollutionEducational2026 documents that pollution drives qualified teachers to migrate away from polluted Chinese cities, depressing local human capital through resource crowding rather than direct cognitive harm. Finally, @weiPhysicalCapitalHuman2022 formalizes these dynamics in an overlapping-generations model in which pollution simultaneously reduces the incentive to invest in schooling (via shortened longevity) and the returns to that investment (via impaired cognition), yielding two stable growth paths and the theoretical possibility that economies become trapped in a persistent low-growth, high-pollution equilibrium.
